transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Liu (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (HelixCare - Head of Platform), Devon Patel (HelixCare - SRE Lead), Lena Okafor (HelixCare - Security Architect)

Summary: short discovery on incident tolerance and regional topology options. HelixCare is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a patient-facing triage and claims summarization workflow. Primary concerns: p99 latency, predictable degradation modes, data residency, and auditability.

Topics: multi-region failover, graceful degradation strategies, model variant fallbacks, SLAs and pilot scope, security artifacts (SOC2 / KMS / SSO).

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Avery Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. apps are in different timezones so appreciate the slot. quick intros, im Avery from Redwood AE. marcus is our se.
[00:10] Marcus Liu: hi all, marcus here, i look after inference arch and SLO design.
[00:15] Marta Ruiz: hi, Marta, Head of Platform at HelixCare. happy to dig in.
[00:19] Devon Patel: Devon, SRE. we run the infra for the triage pipeline.
[00:22] Lena Okafor: Lena, security architect. i'll be focused on compliance and KMS.
[00:25] Marcus Liu: great. quick framing: we're here to map HelixCare's reliability requirements to Redwood options — hosted API, dedicated pools, or private VPC. then we can propose a pilot tailored to your tolerance for incidents.

[03:07] Marta Ruiz: high level, we need the patient triage to be up during office hours in US east and EU west. latency target is p95 < 120ms and p99 ideally under 400ms. cost matters but availability and predictability come first.
[03:28] Devon Patel: to add, during major provider outages we need automated fallback so there is no total outage for our users. we can tolerate reduced model quality for a brief window but not total request failures.
[03:40] Marcus Liu: ok that's helpful. two patterns we recommend: fast path + degradation path. fast path is your primary model served in the nearest region. degradation path can be either: 1) smaller/quantized variant in same region or 2) fail over to another region with traffic steering. both reduce chance of 5xx.

[04:55] Lena Okafor: about data residency — some PII can't leave EU. how does Redwood handle that if we do cross-region fallback?
[05:07] Avery Chen: good question. with Hosted we have configurable routing policies and can restrict per-route region constraints. for strict residency you might use Redwood Private with a VPC that locks data to a region. for hybrid we can do model fan-out: compute stays in EU, but non-PII requests can go to other regions.
[05:31] Marta Ruiz: that sounds like you have multiple knobs. what kind of fallbacks are automated vs manual? we dont want on-call 3am paging for capacity blips.
[05:42] Marcus Liu: our control plane supports automatic fallback policies: if latency or error rate breaches threshold (configurable at route level), traffic can be routed to a canary model, a smaller quantized model, or to a warm standby in another region. you can set cool-downs, circuit-breaker windows, and percentage-based traffic shifts.

[07:15] Devon Patel: warm standby—does that mean you keep a dedicated pool in standby? costs become a concern there.
[07:23] Marcus Liu: two modes: warm standby (reserved instances in Dedicated) for strict SLOs, or a cold/warm hybrid where we keep a smaller dedicated footprint and spin up burst capacity during incidents. with hosted, we can have prewarmed containers for your account to reduce spin-up time. costs differ but you get behavioural guarantees for failover time.

[08:40] Marta Ruiz: in an outage where a region is down, what's the expected RTO to have traffic served from another region?
[08:48] Marcus Liu: depends on the strategy: a prewarmed cross-region standby can take under 60s to take full traffic for small models; if we need to spin new instances in a different region it can be 3–15 minutes depending on GPU availability and model size. we typically advise keeping a lightweight fallback model prewarmed for critical routes.

[10:12] Lena Okafor: what about state — session context or KV cache — when routing cross-region?
[10:20] Marcus Liu: good point. we suggest prefix KV cache replication or sticky session routing. for strict consistency we keep session affinity for active conversations; for cold failover we replay prefix context and accept a short warm-up period where p99 may spike. we also support customer-managed Redis/kv replication in Private deployments.

[11:55] Devon Patel: sounds like we need to model how quality drops with fallback. do you provide tools to simulate degradation?
[12:04] Marcus Liu: yes, Redwood Optimize includes synthetic traffic replay and scorecards. we can run chaos-like simulations for traffic split behaviour, also offer regression alerts tied to prompt suites — so you can see exactly how output drift looks when switching to quantized variants.

[13:30] Marta Ruiz: SLA specifics — what's Redwood's uptime SLA for hosted vs dedicated? and how do you measure latency SLOs?
[13:39] Avery Chen: Hosted has a baseline uptime SLA of 99.9% with credits; Dedicated can go to 99.95% with reserved capacity commitments. latency SLOs are route-level and we report p50/p95/p99 with token-level breakdowns in the Console. for enterprise customers we also offer negotiated SLAs in the contract.

[14:58] Devon Patel: when you say 99.95% for Dedicated, is that across single region or multi-region?
[15:05] Avery Chen: that's for the capacity footprint you reserve. if you reserve across two regions with active-active then you can achieve higher effective availability; the SLA applies to the service for the reserved pool. we can model combined SLOs for multi-region deployments as part of the pilot.

[16:20] Marta Ruiz: compliance artifacts — SOC2 reports, penetration testing, audit logs — can we get those?
[16:27] Lena Okafor: we need audit logs for every inference request with masked payloads, and KMS integration for keys.
[16:34] Marcus Liu: yes, we provide request-level audit logs, TTL masking tools, and KMS/HSM integrations. for Private deployments the control plane can be customer-managed; keys remain in your KMS. we'll share SOC 2 and the network diagrams.

[18:05] Devon Patel: what about partial degradation modes — e.g., degrade to a shorter generation or fall back to a classification-only path?
[18:13] Marcus Liu: you can define route-level degraded outputs: shorter max tokens, different temperature, or swap the model to a distilled/extractive summarizer rather than a full generative transformer. we often do a two-stage fallback: first try a quantized variant, then switch to extractive if quality drops below threshold.

[19:50] Marta Ruiz: can we do traffic split testing during normal ops to prove it doesn't regress?
[19:56] Marcus Liu: absolutely — canary rollouts and A/B testing are built-in. we capture metrics and output diffs. we can gate rollouts based on regression thresholds.

[21:10] Devon Patel: network topology question: if we go Private in our cloud, do you still manage the inference runtime or do we?
[21:18] Avery Chen: private comes in two forms: VPC private control plane (we manage runtime but it's in your VPC) or on-prem install (you manage). most customers choose Redwood Private (customer VPC) for compliance: we manage updates and runtime but everything sits in your network.

[22:48] Lena Okafor: encryption in transit — do you support mTLS inside the cluster and between regions?
[22:54] Marcus Liu: yes, mTLS and strict TLS for inter-region traffic, and we can route via your transit gateway. logs are optionally shipped to your SIEM.

[24:12] Marta Ruiz: i want to understand the expected notification model during incidents — do you push alerts, and what's your escalation path?
[24:20] Marcus Liu: Redwood has webhook alerting to your pager, and we can integrate with opsgenie/splunk. for Dedicated customers we offer a 24/7 support add-on with an on-call rota and SLAs for incident ack and mitigation.

[25:40] Devon Patel: i have a specific scenario: large traffic spike from a marketing campaign, native region saturated. we'd prefer traffic steering to other regions rather than shedding. how fast can that be applied?
[25:52] Marcus Liu: traffic steering rules can be updated dynamically via the Console or API. for automated burst policies we can set thresholds to start shifting X% per minute. if you want immediate manual shift, it takes <15s for routing config to propagate for sessions that aren't sticky. sticky sessions will continue to their original pod until expiration.

[27:30] Marta Ruiz: what's the observability retention for request traces and cost logs?
[27:36] Avery Chen: Console defaults to 30 days for detailed traces, and we have paid retention plans up to a year. cost logs include token-level breakdown and model cost. for Private you can ship logs to your S3 or SIEM.

[29:02] Devon Patel: any gotchas with HTTP timeouts or long-running streaming responses? we have some long conversations that last minutes.
[29:10] Marcus Liu: streaming is supported; we recommend per-route stream timeouts and progressive KV cache commits. long sessions are sticky; token cache size matters. very long sequences can increase latency — we suggest session summarization or checkpointing to control cache size.

[31:00] Marta Ruiz: can you walk us through a simple topology recommendation for us?
[31:08] Marcus Liu: sure. Recommendation A (hosted hybrid): primary hosted cluster in us-east and eu-west with prewarmed quantized fallbacks in each region; route policy restricts PII to EU for eu-based customers. Recommendation B (dedicated reserved): reserved dedicated pools in each region + a small warm standby in a third region for fast failover, higher cost but stronger RTO. Recommendation C (private): customer VPC in EU for residency-critical traffic, Redwood-managed control plane, and a hosted fallback in US for non-PII.

[33:12] Marta Ruiz: i like B for core triage and C for records processing maybe. cost team will push back. can we run an experiment to quantify degrade quality and cost delta?
[33:22] Marcus Liu: yes, pilot: run your sample traffic against our hosted baseline and a quantized fallback. we'll replay a day of production traffic and output cost/quality deltas and p99 latency plots.

[35:05] Devon Patel: workload profile: 60% short prompts (~50 tokens), 30% medium, 10% long. mostly US east and EU west. we'll share exact numbers.

[35:34] Lena Okafor: for the pilot, i will need the SOC2, network diagram, and KMS integration guide.

[36:02] Avery Chen: we'll send those. Marcus, can you also include the runbook template?
[36:08] Marcus Liu: yep i'll attach the multi-region failover runbook and a sample policy YAML.

[37:45] Marta Ruiz: one last question, does Redwood support per-route RBAC so product teams can't change global fallback policies?
[37:53] Marcus Liu: yes, role-based controls in Console; you can separate route config from project-level settings and lock fallback orchestration to platform admins.

[39:00] Devon Patel: any limitations on model types for fallback? can we fallback from a Llama-3-like model to a smaller distilled model?
[39:07] Marcus Liu: yes, as long as the model family is compatible and we've verified the tokenizer/seq behavior. we maintain compatibility matrices and can advise on best fallback pairs.

[40:22] Marta Ruiz: perfect. let's recap and close.
[40:28] Avery Chen: recap: Redwood to run benchmarks on hosted small model, share SOC2/KMS docs and network diagrams, send runbook and sample policy YAML, and propose pilot scope & pricing. HelixCare to send traffic profile and confirm residency constraints.
[41:05] Marcus Liu: i'll run the synthetic replay and send p99 plots; i'll also include example degraded output so you can measure quality drop.
[41:18] Lena Okafor: i'll confirm KMS vendor and policy, aim to respond by Friday.
[41:25] Devon Patel: i'll push traffic numbers by tomorrow.

[41:35] Marta Ruiz: thanks — appreciate the concrete options. we'll aim for an internal decision next week.

[57:45] Avery Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with artifacts.

-- End --

Notes: transcript contains typical ASR artifacts (some names slightly off in auto transcript). Shared artifacts referenced: multi-region-failover-runbook.pdf (will be shared), SOC2-report.pdf, pilot-pricing-sheet.xlsx.

- Redwood SE: run benchmark with HelixCare traffic replay, share p99/p95/p50 plots and degraded-output diff (Marcus)
